alg-gr-fx-periodic-wave-leapfrog:
## Definition

Use the first circle factor of the fixed periodic three-torus from the earlier
fixed-gauge data definition. This item is a separate nondimensionalized scalar
model: both the spatial coordinate $x$ and time $t$ are dimensionless, the
period is $2\pi$, and the model wave speed is $1$. Let $N\ge3$ be an integer,
$h:=2\pi/N$, and $x_j:=jh\pmod{2\pi}$ for $j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$. A
periodic grid function is an $N$-tuple $u=(u_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z}$ of
real numbers. Define the centered periodic second-difference operator
$$
(D_hu)_j:=\frac{u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}}{h^2},
$$
where subscripts are reduced modulo $N$.

The algorithm takes as input such arrays $u^0,v^0$, a real time step $k>0$,
and an integer $n_{\max}\ge1$. It sets
$$
u^1:=u^0+kv^0+\frac{k^2}{2}D_hu^0,
$$
then, for each integer $n=1,\ldots,n_{\max}-1$, computes
$$
u^{n+1}_j:=2u^n_j-u^{n-1}_j+k^2(D_hu^n)_j \qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z).
$$
It outputs $(u^0,u^1,\ldots,u^{n_{\max}})$. All operations here are exact real
arithmetic. No rounding-error model or claim about a floating-point
implementation is part of the definition.
prop-gr-fx-leapfrog-termination:
## Statement

For every admissible integer $N\ge3$, time-step count $n_{\max}\ge1$, real
step $k>0$, and pair of real periodic input arrays, the algorithm terminates
after exactly $n_{\max}-1$ update passes and outputs all levels through
$u^{n_{\max}}$. In the unit-cost exact-real-arithmetic model, where each scalar
arithmetic operation and each array read or write has bounded cost independent
of $N$ and $n_{\max}$, its operation count is $O(Nn_{\max})$.
thm-gr-fx-leapfrog-mode-stability:
## Statement

Let $N\ge3$, $h=2\pi/N$, $k>0$, and $\lambda=k/h$. Complexify the real
linear recurrence of the periodic wave algorithm. For each discrete Fourier
index $\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}$ define the mode
$$
e_\ell(j):=\exp(2\pi i\ell j/N),\qquad j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z.
$$
If $0<\lambda<1$, every nonconstant mode ($\ell\ne0$) has recurrence
coefficient
$$
c_\ell:=1-2\lambda^2\sin^2(\pi\ell/N)\in(-1,1)
$$
and two distinct amplification roots
$$
z_{\ell,\pm}:=c_\ell\pm i\sqrt{1-c_\ell^2},\qquad |z_{\ell,\pm}|=1.
$$
Consequently, each fixed nonconstant mode has bounded amplitude on every
finite slab. For arbitrary real initial arrays define their spatial means by
$$
\bar u^0:=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}u^0_j,\qquad \bar v^0:=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}v^0_j.
$$
The constant mode has the repeated root $1$ and evolves exactly as
$\bar u^0+nk\bar v^0$; for any fixed $T\ge0$ it is bounded on the slab
$0\le nk\le T$ but has no uniform-in-time displacement bound when
$\bar v^0\ne0$. This statement
does not assert that the condition $0<\lambda<1$ alone proves convergence of a
numerical relativity scheme. For each fixed $N$, define the nonzero discrete
frequencies $\omega_\ell:=2h^{-1}|\sin(\pi\ell/N)|$, $1\le\ell<N$.
This finite list has a positive minimum; it is a fixed-grid fact and no bound
uniform in $N$ is asserted.
For even $N$, the alternating mode with Fourier index $\ell=N/2$ is called
the Nyquist mode. At the endpoint $\lambda=1$, if $N$ is even and
$u_j^0=a_0(-1)^j$, $v_j^0=\beta_0(-1)^j$ for real amplitudes $a_0,\beta_0$,
then each output level satisfies
$$
u_j^n=(-1)^j(-1)^n(a_0-nk\beta_0).
$$
The Nyquist amplification root is repeated at $-1$, and a nonzero Nyquist
velocity amplitude $\beta_0$ gives linear growth in the step number.
thm-gr-fx-leapfrog-local-truncation:
## Statement

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, and let $u:I\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$
be six times continuously differentiable and $2\pi$-periodic in its spatial
variable $x$. Assume the nondimensional scalar wave equation
$u_{tt}=u_{xx}$ on $I\times\mathbb R$. For $N\ge3$, $h=2\pi/N$, $k>0$,
$x_j=jh$, and an integer $n$ with $t_n=nk$ and
$[t_n-k,t_n+k]\subset I$, put
$$
U_j^n:=u(x_j,t_n),\qquad \tau_j^n:=\frac{U_j^{n+1}-2U_j^n+U_j^{n-1}}{k^2} -\frac{U_{j+1}^n-2U_j^n+U_{j-1}^n}{h^2}.
$$
Set $M_n$ to be the supremum
$$
M_n:=\sup\{|\partial_x^4u(x,t)|:0\le x\le2\pi,\ t_n-k\le t\le t_n+k\}.
$$
Then for every grid index $j$,
$$
|\tau_j^n|\le\frac{k^2+h^2}{12}M_n.
$$
Thus the normalized local truncation residual is $O(k^2+h^2)$ on each
compact time window where the displayed fourth-derivative bound is uniform.
This consistency estimate alone is not a convergence theorem.
def-gr-fx-constraint-residual-diagnostic:
## Definition

Use the dimensionless angular coordinates $x^i$ and the periodic spatial
three-torus from the earlier fixed-gauge data definition. Choose integers
$N_i\ge3$, coordinate spacings $\Delta_i:=2\pi/N_i$, and the finite periodic
grid
$$
G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=\{(2\pi j_1/N_1,2\pi j_2/N_2,2\pi j_3/N_3): 0\le j_i<N_i\}\subset\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}.
$$
At each grid node $p$, supply a real symmetric positive-definite matrix
$h_{ij}(p)$ and its matrix inverse $h^{ij}(p)$ (so
$h^{ik}(p)h_{kj}(p)=\delta^i{}_j$), a real symmetric array $K_{ij}(p)$,
a scalar $\rho(p)$, a covector array $j_i(p)$, and real constants $\Lambda$
and $\kappa>0$. These are the sampled spatial metric, second fundamental
form, energy density and momentum density in the convention of
[[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]]: for a future unit normal $n$
and the coordinate basis $\partial_i$, $K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_Xn,Y)$,
$\rho=T(n,n)$ and $j_i=-T(n,\partial_i)$, where $T$ is a smooth symmetric
covariant two-tensor. The array definition itself needs only the listed
samples and does not assume the continuum field equation. The vacuum case is
$\rho=j_i=\Lambda=0$. In the SI angular-coordinate convention used here,
$[x^i]=1$, $[h_{ij}]=\mathrm m^2$, $[K_{ij}]=\mathrm m$,
$[\rho]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, $[j_i]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-2}}$,
$[\Lambda]=\mathrm m^{-2}$, and
$[\kappa]=\mathrm{m^{-1}\,kg^{-1}\,s^2}$. Thus the scalar residual below
has units $\mathrm m^{-2}$ and its covector components in this angular basis
have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

Let $\mathbb R^{G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}}$ denote the real arrays indexed by
the grid. Choose and specify linear maps
$\delta_i:\mathbb R^{G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}}\to
\mathbb R^{G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}}$ with $\delta_i1=0$; apply them
componentwise to tensor arrays. Periodic index wrapping is used here. Define
the discrete connection components, curvature, Ricci array and scalar
curvature by nodewise operations, with every index $i,j,k,\ell,a,b$ ranging
over $1,2,3$ and repeated upper/lower indices summed:
$$
\Gamma^k{}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}:= \frac12h^{k\ell}(\delta_i h_{j\ell}+\delta_j h_{i\ell}-\delta_\ell h_{ij}),
$$
$$
R^a{}_{b i j,\boldsymbol\Delta}:= \delta_i\Gamma^a{}_{jb,\boldsymbol\Delta} -\delta_j\Gamma^a{}_{ib,\boldsymbol\Delta} +\Gamma^a{}_{i\ell,\boldsymbol\Delta}\Gamma^\ell{}_{jb,\boldsymbol\Delta} -\Gamma^a{}_{j\ell,\boldsymbol\Delta}\Gamma^\ell{}_{ib,\boldsymbol\Delta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}:=R^k{}_{i k j,\boldsymbol\Delta}, \qquad R_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=h^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}.
$$
Set
$$
\tau_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=h^{ij}K_{ij},\qquad |K|^2_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=h^{ik}h^{j\ell}K_{ij}K_{k\ell},
$$
$$
(D_i^{\boldsymbol\Delta}K)_{kj}:= \delta_iK_{kj}-\Gamma^\ell{}_{ik,\boldsymbol\Delta}K_{\ell j} -\Gamma^\ell{}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}K_{k\ell}.
$$
The signed discrete Hamiltonian and momentum residuals are
$$
\mathcal H_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:= R_{\boldsymbol\Delta}+\tau_{\boldsymbol\Delta}^2 -|K|^2_{\boldsymbol\Delta}-2\Lambda-2\kappa\rho,
$$
$$
\mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta,j}:= h^{ik}(D_i^{\boldsymbol\Delta}K)_{kj} -\delta_j\tau_{\boldsymbol\Delta}+\kappa j_j.
$$
These signs match the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints in
[[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]] when its pointwise equation
$G+\Lambda g=\kappa T$ is assumed. The displayed discrete formulas are array
operations: they do not define a coordinate-covariant discrete connection or
assume a discrete Leibniz rule. A reconstruction map has the exact type
$$
\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:\mathcal D_{\boldsymbol\Delta}\longrightarrow \mathcal C,
$$
where $\mathcal D_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$ is the set of all grid arrays
$(h_{ij},K_{ij},\rho,j_i)$ with the pointwise symmetry and positive-definite
conditions above, and $\mathcal C$ is the set of pointwise assignments on
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ of a positive-definite symmetric covariant two-tensor
$h$, a symmetric covariant two-tensor $K$, a scalar $\rho$ and a covector
$j$, with the same units. No continuity or differentiability of a member of
$\mathcal C$ is implied; if continuum derivatives are used, the needed
regularity must be stated separately. Specify $\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$
as part of each diagnostic, since it records which continuum field the grid
is intended to represent. For every reported diagnostic, also record the grid
norm and its weights, the mesh hierarchy, the units, the derivative maps, the
periodic boundary treatment, and $\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$. A small
residual by itself does not assert closeness to an exact constraint-satisfying
development.
ex-gr-fx11-1:
## Statement

Let $N\ge4$ be even, let $h=2\pi/N$, and choose the Courant--Friedrichs--Lewy
(CFL) step ratio $\lambda:=k/h>1$. Run the periodic wave algorithm with
$u_j^0=(-1)^j$ and $v_j^0=0$, with any integer $n_{\max}\ge1$. For every integer
$0\le n\le n_{\max}$ the output has the form $u_j^n=a_n(-1)^j$, where, with
$c:=1-2\lambda^2<-1$,
$$
a_n=\frac{z_{\rm grow}^n+z_{\rm decay}^n}{2},\qquad z_{\rm grow}:=c-\sqrt{c^2-1}<-1,\qquad z_{\rm decay}:=c+\sqrt{c^2-1}\in(-1,0).
$$
Consequently $|a_n|\ge |z_{\rm grow}|^n/2$, so allowing more time steps
causes exponential growth of this alternating mode. The strict hypothesis
$0<k/h<1$ in the preceding mode theorem excludes this example; no endpoint
claim at $k/h=1$ is made here.
